records.sourceFile: Plant-based diets and sports performance - A clinical review.pdf

paper.citation: Maier SP, Lightsey HM, Galetta MD, Usoro AO, Oh LS. Plant-based diets and sports performance: a clinical review. Sport Sciences for Health. 2023.
paper.abstract: This clinical review examines plant-based diets in relation to athletic performance, drawing on systematic reviews, randomized trials and cohort studies. The authors report no significant difference in strength, power or aerobic and anaerobic performance between plant-based and omnivorous diets. They note that plant-based diets carry higher risks of micronutrient deficiency, reduced protein intake, and lower serum creatine and testosterone, and that supplementation may replace the missing components.
paper.tldr: A clinical review finds no consistent performance difference between plant-based and omnivorous diets for strength, power and endurance in the studies it assembled. Plant-based diets carry higher risks of micronutrient shortfalls and lower creatine, so athletes need planned nutrition and supplementation.
paper.methods: A single author searched PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE and Google Scholar using combinations of athlete, diet, vegan, vegetarian, performance and related terms, reducing 232 hits to 36 sources after abstract review. Sources included systematic reviews, randomized trials, cohort and cross-sectional studies, and case reports, summarized in Table 1 by study type, level of evidence, sample and findings.
paper.findings: Strength studies in older and younger men (19 to 38 participants per trial) showed no consistent between-diet difference, though one trial found a larger knee extension gain on the vegetarian diet and another found lower fat-free and muscle mass on the vegetarian diet in men aged 51 to 69. Endurance evidence is mixed: in eight endurance-trained men, a vegetarian diet lowered testosterone without changing VO2max or time to exhaustion, nine recreational men showed about 13% higher oxygen consumption at submaximal cycling, and a study of 27 vegetarian and 43 omnivorous elite endurance athletes is described as showing higher oxygen consumption in vegetarians, while its Table 1 entry also reports no group difference and higher peak oxygen intake only in female vegetarians. Creatine studies found lower baseline muscle creatine in vegetarians (18 vs 24 participants), and creatine supplementation raised bench press by 19% compared with 11% for placebo, with no difference between diets in that response.
paper.limitations: The authors note that the included studies vary in size, design, outcomes and population, and that most trials last 6 to 12 weeks, which may be too short to show adaptation. Two Haub entries in Table 1 describe samples of the same size and age (21 older men), so they may share a cohort, and the Lynch et al. 2016 entry is internally inconsistent (higher oxygen consumption '53% vs 47%' in the text versus 'no difference in oxygen consumption' and female peak values of 53.0 vs 47.1 in the table). Table 1 describes the Burke et al. creatine study as protein supplementation in vegetarians, while the narrative describes creatine supplementation, so the intervention is unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes on plant-based diets should have protein, micronutrient and creatine intake checked, and the review advises supplementation as needed, including vitamin B12 for plant-based dieters and creatine where intake is low. Protein targets should be set against sport-specific estimates, which the review cites as around 1.9 g/kg/day for athletes, rather than general population values. The review's main recommendation is a nutritionally sufficient diet regardless of source.
paper.athleteDev: In the studies reviewed, plant-based and omnivorous athletes did not show consistent differences in strength or power, so diet type alone does not clearly limit performance. Endurance findings are mixed, with higher oxygen cost at submaximal exercise reported in some studies, and creatine supplementation is the main compensating strategy in the strength studies.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. Its illness and energy availability sections describe infection risk in Olympic athletes but do not set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Popular dietary trends impact on athletic performance - A critical analysis review.pdf

paper.citation: Kaufman M, Nguyen C, Shetty M, Oppezzo M, Barrack M, Fredericson M. Popular Dietary Trends' Impact on Athletic Performance: A Critical Analysis Review. Nutrients. 2023;15:3511.
paper.abstract: A review, described by the authors as narrative, of research on five common diets (Mediterranean, ketogenic, low-carbohydrate, plant-based and intermittent fasting) and athletic performance, with notes on risks such as micronutrient deficiency and disordered eating. The authors conclude that no single diet suits all athletes and that athletes should review any diet change with a medical professional.
paper.tldr: No diet is clearly superior for athletic performance, and the main risks are nutrient shortfalls, poor adherence and disordered eating. Athletes considering a diet change should involve a sports dietitian and monitor their health and performance.
paper.methods: Review of the five most common diet patterns, using PubMed searches for narrative and systematic reviews and meta-analyses from 2015-2022 plus the primary studies cited in them. Additional articles were used to propose an initial eating disorder risk assessment. No search terms, selection criteria, study flow or quality appraisal are reported.
paper.findings: The authors report performance gains from the Mediterranean diet in small studies without control groups and no performance decrement from ketogenic or low-carbohydrate diets in several trials, with reduced body mass in some. One systematic review found no performance differences between plant-based and omnivorous athletes, while a later review reported some differences, including greater gains in muscle mass and creatine stores in meat eaters. Intermittent fasting was linked to slower sprints, reduced time to exhaustion and slower rowing in some studies, especially during Ramadan or multi-day fasts, while a large review of overnight fasts found minimal performance differences.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe search terms, study selection or risk-of-bias assessment, and it relies on many small or short studies that the authors describe as limited. The conclusion says intermittent fasting decreases athletic performance, a firmer claim than the body text's 'varying results', and the protein range in the conclusion (1.2-1.7 g/kg/day) differs from Section 3.1 (1.2-2.0 g/kg/day). The sample meal plans are illustrative rather than tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes and staff can use the paper's framework to check whether a diet meets energy, carbohydrate, protein and micronutrient needs; the authors cite 6-10 g/kg carbohydrate and 1.2-1.7 g/kg protein as general targets. Vegan or vegetarian athletes should monitor vitamin B12, vitamin D, iron, zinc, calcium and protein, and restrictive or fasting plans should be checked for energy availability and disordered eating risk with a registered dietitian.
paper.athleteDev: Performance evidence for each diet mostly comes from small studies, so a diet change should be trialed with monitoring of training quality and body mass rather than assumed to improve performance. Energy availability and continued resistance training are the most relevant points for performance.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review does not address injury rehabilitation or return criteria, and its injury-related remarks, such as bone health and healing with micronutrient deficiency, are general and untested.

records.sourceFile: Post-exercise rehydration in athletes - Effects of sodium and carbohydrate in commercial hydration beverages.pdf

paper.citation: Ly NQ, Hamstra-Wright KL, Horswill CA. Post-Exercise Rehydration in Athletes: Effects of Sodium and Carbohydrate in Commercial Hydration Beverages. Nutrients. 2023;15:4759.
paper.abstract: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial compared water, an oral rehydration solution and a sports drink for fluid retention after about 2.6% body mass loss in 26 trained men. Both the ORS and sports drink retained more fluid than water at 3.5 h, and they did not differ from each other. The authors report that the early rehydration pattern favored the ORS.
paper.tldr: After losing about 2.6% of body mass, a 2.5% carbohydrate, 45 mmol/L sodium ORS and a 6% carbohydrate, 18 mmol/L sports drink both retained more fluid than water over 3.5 h, with no difference between them. Both drinks cut urine output versus water within the first hour, so the authors' claim of an early ORS advantage is weakly supported.
paper.methods: Randomized, counterbalanced, double-blind crossover design with three trials (up to 3 weeks apart for the first 20 participants, 3 days apart for the final six). Participants exercised without fluid for about 90 min, rested 45 min, then drank a volume equal to 100% of mass lost over 1 h. Urine was collected at 30, 60, 135 and 210 min, and percent fluid retained over 3.5 h was the primary outcome; a pilot sub-sample of the final six participants also had forearm sweat sodium measured to estimate sodium balance.
paper.findings: Percent fluid retained at 3.5 h was 58.1 +/- 12.6% for water, 73.9 +/- 10.9% for the sports drink and 76.9 +/- 8.0% for the ORS, with both drinks higher than water (P<0.05) and not different from each other. In the Results, water produced more urine than the sports drink at 30 min and more than both drinks at 60 min, with a faster early suppression of urine output for the ORS than the sports drink. In the six-participant sub-sample, sodium balance correlated with fluid retained (r=0.49, P<0.05, 18 non-independent observations), while fluid retained differed only as a trend across drinks (P=0.06).
paper.limitations: Only trained men were studied, in a laboratory with a single 3.5 h endpoint, and the authors note that the forearm sweat-sodium method may overestimate loss. The sodium-balance correlation pools three trials from each of six participants, which the authors acknowledge violates independence. The study was funded by the EAS Division of Abbott Nutrition, and the corresponding author received honoraria from EAS and Abbott Nutrition; the authors state the funder had no role. The abstract says the sports drink did not differ from water early on, but the Results report less sports-drink urine than water at 30 and 60 min; the Discussion osmolality values (ORS 260, sports drink 335-350) also differ from Table 3 (270 and 330-380 mOsm/kg).
paper.practicalImplications: When athletes must rehydrate within about 3.5 h after losing about 2.6% of body mass, the trial supports a sodium- and carbohydrate-containing drink over water alone; after water, participants were still about 2% below starting mass versus 1.3% (ORS) and 1.5% (sports drink). The 3.5 h retention did not separate the ORS and sports drink, so the choice between them can rest on sugar and energy intake. The authors' claims of an early ORS advantage and of a sodium-balance benefit rest on secondary and pilot data.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured fluid retention, not performance. It does not show that either drink improves performance in a later session, although the authors cite literature linking dehydration of about 2% to reduced endurance and cognition.
paper.rtp: The study does not involve injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. Its relevance is rehydration between training sessions or competitions, not rehabilitation or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Prevalence of adulteration in dietary supplements and recommendations for safe supplement practices in sport.pdf

paper.citation: Jagim AR, Harty PS, Erickson JL, Tinsley GM, Garner D, Galpin AJ. Prevalence of adulteration in dietary supplements and recommendations for safe supplement practices in sport. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;5:1239121.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of dietary supplement adulteration and mislabelling, the risk of inadvertent doping in athletes, and safe supplementation practices. It summarises analytical studies of supplements sold in the US, reports that 14% to 50% of analysed products tested positive for anabolic agents or other prohibited substances, and sets out practical steps for athletes.
paper.tldr: Analytical studies find undeclared stimulants and anabolic agents in many supplements, which creates a real risk of inadvertent doping for drug-tested athletes. Risk is reduced by choosing third-party verified products, checking ingredients against the current prohibited list, and keeping product lot records.
paper.methods: Review described by the authors as narrative. Sources were PubMed, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus and Google Scholar, searched with terms on supplements, ergogenic aids, adulteration, doping, contamination and athletes, plus a manual check of reference lists. The authors state that a systematic review and meta-analysis were not possible because of the heterogeneity of the evidence, and no screening counts or quality appraisal are reported.
paper.findings: Table 1 summarises US-market analytical studies from 1998 to 2023 that found prohibited or unapproved stimulants and steroids, and one review of 875 supplements reported sibutramine in 28.3%, testosterone or other anabolic steroids in 26.1% and fluoxetine in 21.4%. In a Norwegian dataset, athletes attributed 49 of 192 anti-doping violations (26%) to a supplement, and supporting urine evidence was found in 27 of those 49. A test of 28 volunteers after travel to China found clenbuterol in 22 (79%) samples, which the authors attribute to possible food contamination.
paper.limitations: No systematic selection, quality appraisal or pooled estimates are reported. The abstract gives 14% to 50% of analysed samples as positive for anabolic agents or other prohibited substances, the body cites a 2017 review with contamination rates of 12% to 58%, and the conclusion gives 10% to 30% of supplements, and the review does not reconcile these ranges. Three authors report consulting for and funding from companies that sell dietary ingredients, and one reports research funding from and paid consulting for sports nutrition companies; the authors state that none of these entities played a role in the article.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes in drug-tested sport should choose products certified by a third-party programme that specifically tests for prohibited substances, while knowing that such programmes cannot test for every listed substance. Ingredients should be checked routinely against the governing body's prohibited list, which is typically updated annually, and drug-tested athletes may retain product samples and lot or batch numbers in case of an appeal. Combining products with overlapping ingredients should be avoided because the total amount of an ingredient can reach high or dangerous levels.
paper.athleteDev: The review covers adulteration and mislabelling rather than training effects and does not assess efficacy in depth. It reports that pre-workout, thermogenic and muscle-building products have the highest reported adulteration and adverse-event rates, so product choice matters within any performance supplement plan.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its relevant point is that supplements can cause inadvertent positive tests, so products should be checked before use by athletes who are being tested.

records.sourceFile: Quality control of protein supplements - A review.pdf

paper.citation: da Costa BRB, Roiffé RR, de la Cruz MNS. Quality Control of Protein Supplements: A Review. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2021 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This review gathers reports on quality problems in sport protein supplements, mainly whey protein. It covers reduced nutritional value from label mismatch and adulteration, undeclared pharmacological substances, and microbial and toxic-metal contamination.
paper.tldr: The review finds frequent gaps between protein labels and actual content, and occasional undeclared drugs, microbes and metals in protein supplements. It advises athletes to use products with a quality seal, because even trace contaminants can cause a positive doping test.
paper.methods: ScienceDirect, PubMed and Web of Science were searched with four terms for studies from January 2005 to July 2020 that performed quality-control analysis of protein supplements. Of 108 abstracts, 81 full texts were assessed and 30 were included, with reference lists of relevant articles also checked. Findings are grouped as reduced nutritional value, pharmacological substances, and microbial and toxic-metal contamination.
paper.findings: Labelled protein content often did not match the product: Schönfeldt et al., as reported in the review, found 68% of 70 high-protein sports supplements statistically different from their label, and Almeida et al. (2016a) found 11 of 20 whey products had lower total protein than labelled. Undeclared substances were reported in whey products, with 7 of 11 Brazilian whey brands adulterated with diuretics or stimulants (Roiffé et al., 2019) and 14 of 44 whey samples containing caffeine that was not on the label (Costa et al., 2020). Clean Label Project (2018) reported detectable lead in 70%, cadmium in 74% and arsenic in 85% of 134 protein products, without stating whether levels exceeded safe limits, while other whey studies cited found metals within regulatory limits.
paper.limitations: The review does not appraise study quality or pool results, and the authors note that some studies of protein supplements may have been missed because many articles treat all samples as 'nutritional supplements' without specifying the type. Many included studies analyse small numbers of products (for example, four protein supplements in De Ceglie et al., 2015), and the review does not claim market-wide prevalence. Blocked lysine and furosine are discussed as possible quality markers, but the review states that more study is needed to decide whether they are appropriate and what cut-offs to use.
paper.practicalImplications: The review advises athletes to use supplements with a quality seal showing they were tested for prohibited substances, and to avoid products that make strong claims about muscle gain or weight loss. It also notes that products can contain less protein than their label states, which may affect diet and performance.
paper.athleteDev: The review links product quality to performance mainly through lower-than-labelled protein and blocked lysine, which may reduce nutritional value, although it says more studies are needed to decide whether blocked lysine is an appropriate quality parameter. Because protein supplements are taken in large daily doses (about 25 to 30 g), trace contaminants could lead to a positive doping test, so the authors advise athletes to choose products with a quality seal.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport or injury. The review concerns supplement quality, contamination and doping risk, and does not assess recovery after injury.
